questions.q: In LTV Global's workforce identity design, what role does Salesforce play relative to Okta?
options: Salesforce acts as the Service Provider, trusting Okta's authentication assertion instead of managing a separate password
Salesforce acts as the Identity Provider, and Okta trusts its assertions
Salesforce and Okta have no relationship; each manages its own separate credentials
Okta is used only for the Experience Cloud dealer portal, never for internal Salesforce users
questions.explain: Okta is the identity provider for LTV Global's ~10,000 internal users; Salesforce is the Service Provider that trusts Okta's SAML assertion rather than managing a competing set of credentials.

questions.q: Why does Salesforce's own MFA requirement not independently fire when a workforce user logs in via SP-initiated SSO from Okta?
options: Because MFA is permanently disabled once SSO is configured
Because Salesforce does not support MFA at all for enterprise customers
Because the burden of strong authentication shifts to Okta, which is only safe if Okta itself is confirmed to enforce MFA for every workforce user
Because My Domain removes the need for MFA entirely
questions.explain: Salesforce's MFA requirement doesn't fire for SSO logins because the authentication burden has shifted to the IdP — which only safely satisfies the intent of the requirement if Okta-side MFA enforcement is explicitly verified, not assumed.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say external identity (dealers and end customers) deliberately does NOT reuse the same corporate Okta relationship as the workforce?
options: Because Okta cannot technically support any external users
Because Okta's workforce licensing and governance model is built and priced for employees, not for millions of consumer logins with no employment relationship
Because Experience Cloud is incompatible with SAML
Because dealers are legally prohibited from using corporate identity providers
questions.explain: The decision is about licensing and scale fit, not technical impossibility — Okta's workforce product isn't designed or priced for millions of consumer logins, and tying portal availability to workforce identity infrastructure also creates unwanted coupling.

questions.q: What is LTV Global's hybrid model for external identity?
options: All dealers and end customers federate through corporate Okta, with no exceptions
Every end customer is issued an internal Salesforce license
No external users are allowed to authenticate at all; everything goes through internal reps
Large dealers may federate their own IdP via SAML into the dealer Experience Cloud site; smaller dealers and individual end customers self-register and authenticate natively through Experience Cloud
questions.explain: The hybrid model matches the identity path to scale and sophistication: large dealers can bring their own IdP, while smaller dealers and millions of individual end customers use Experience Cloud's native self-registration and login.

questions.q: How does this lesson frame the decision not to route all external identity through corporate Okta, in terms of Chapter 6 preparation?
options: As a rejected alternative, explicitly named and defended with the real reason (licensing/scale mismatch) it was rejected, rather than just describing the chosen design
As an irrelevant detail that will not come up during the ARB defense
As a mistake the architect made that should be hidden from the review board
As a decision that has nothing to do with the chosen hybrid federation model
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames routing everyone through corporate Okta as a considered-and-rejected alternative, with the specific reason for rejection (licensing/scale mismatch) ready to defend in Chapter 6 — exactly the kind of reasoning an ARB probes for.
